prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and to the microfounded, rule-based analysis of monetary policy.

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I still rate B015 as the strongest case on the shortlist, and I judge it on scientific grounds rather than on how many colleagues ranked it first. Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework supply the common language in which monetary policy is analysed in academia and in central banks. Calvo's tractable time-dependent pricing and Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule are original building blocks. Woodford's work turned them into an integrated, welfare-based theory of policy that connects the micro foundations to the way policy is conducted. The framework has been revised and extended through the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation without being displaced, and a framework that survives such tests is a good sign of durable scientific content. The trio is the one case on the list where the originators of the key components and the synthesiser can be named cleanly, even though other names also have real claims.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the strongest reservation. Eight names are credited and the work is a collective research programme. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, among others, were central to turning the theory into an estimated, policy-ready model. A three-name prize therefore credits the originators and the synthesiser while leaving out those who made the framework quantitatively usable. Calvo's and Taylor's key papers are also much older than the synthesis, so the trio spans four decades. There is also a substantive worry that the simple representative-agent framework did not clearly anticipate the 2008 financial frictions or the 2021-23 inflation dynamics, and that heterogeneous-agent extensions partly challenge it. A prize must credit what has been established, and this one risks reading as a recognition of a paradigm whose limits are still being mapped.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B015 first with the same Woodford, Taylor, Calvo trio. He sees a natural split between staggered pricing and contracts on one side and Woodford's integrated framework on the other. He also flags that choosing three from a crowded field is contestable and that the post-2021 inflation has prompted debate about the simple framework.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of the credit and I share the worry about the post-2021 episode. I would add that the framework's endurance rests partly on its being extendable. Financial frictions and household heterogeneity have been added to it without overturning the core pricing and policy-rule logic, and that supports the claim of a durable discovery. I would not rely on Hassler's agreement as evidence, since we are long-standing co-authors and I treat that as a disclosed tie. Where I would press him is on whether Calvo and Taylor should be regarded as one contribution or two. I think the citation is cleaner if they are framed as the origin of nominal rigidity and the policy rule, with Woodford as the synthesis.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B015 second with Woodford, Galí and Taylor. He values Galí's empirical and theoretical development of the framework and notes that Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have strong claims.
responses.response: Galí's claim is real, particularly through the canonical New Keynesian model and the empirical work on the Phillips curve and on monetary transmission. I still prefer Calvo in the third slot because the Calvo pricing mechanism is the building block on which much of the later analysis, including Galí's, rests. Galí's work is largely a development of that structure. This is a judgement about originality versus development, and I accept that the reverse ordering is defensible. I would not call it a mistake to put Galí ahead of Calvo. I concede that choosing Calvo risks under-crediting the people who made the framework empirically usable, and I record that cost rather than dismissing it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B015 fourth, behind B038, B050 and B016. He thinks Woodford, Galí and Gertler is the most coherent trio for the theory plus policy implications, and he notes that credit is widely dispersed and that Gertler appears on two ballots.
responses.response: Boppart is right that Gertler's presence on B015 and B050 blurs the credit, and that is an argument against building a B015 trio around him. His trio emphasises the theory-plus-estimation side. Mine emphasises the origin of the mechanisms plus the synthesis. Neither is arbitrary, but the origin-based version is easier to defend if the question is who established the idea. I do not accept that dispersed credit makes B015 a weaker scientific case than B038. Dispersed credit complicates the prize design but does not reduce the scientific importance. B038 has a cleaner Melitz-Helpman core, and that is a real advantage. I treat it as the main alternative and not as a reason to lower B015.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B050 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that collateral constraints turn small shocks into persistent, amplified credit cycles, that this became a workhorse after 2008, and that attribution to the two authors is clean. He also notes that direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is more mixed than its theoretical influence suggests.
responses.response: I find the B050 case serious, and the clean two-name attribution is a genuine strength that B015 lacks. The mechanism is foundational for macro-finance. Where I differ is on breadth of impact. The collateral-constraint mechanism has shaped research, but the nominal-rigidity framework has shaped both research and day-to-day policy practice. Strömberg's own caveat about empirical identification and the overlap with the 2022 prize also weigh on the marginal case. I would not call B050 weaker in originality. I weigh policy reach and tested durability a little higher, and I accept that a committee that values clean attribution above breadth could reasonably reverse my ordering.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo or Galí is the better third name, and whether a three-name limit can fairly represent a programme with at least eight credited contributors.

How much the framework's performance in 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation should lower its standing as an established discovery, and how much heterogeneous-agent extensions complement or challenge it.
How to treat the overlap with earlier macroeconomics prizes on expectations, policy and business cycles when defining the incremental contribution.
Whether the B038 or B050 cases, which have cleaner attribution, should outrank B015 if attribution clarity is weighted above breadth of impact.
My assessments rest on my general knowledge and the supplied evidence, not on independent verification of the record.
statement.conflict_note: Nothing in my supplied profile connects me to Woodford, Taylor or Calvo. The profile does show long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (committee chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member), both of whom comment on B015 and other ballots, and I treat these as disclosed ties that I have not adjudicated. My own research in heterogeneous-agent macroeconomics could bias me for or against a representative-agent framework, so I have applied the same criteria as for the other fields. My opening mentioned an institutional tie to Torsten Persson, which my supplied profile does not establish. I do not propose B021 and have kept it out of my alternatives for that reason.
